questions.stem: Which equation represents the steam reforming of methane?
options: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)
2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
CO(g) + H₂O(g) → CO₂(g) + H₂(g)
CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + 3H₂(g)
questions.explanation: In steam reforming, methane reacts with steam over a nickel catalyst to give carbon monoxide and hydrogen. The second equation is combustion, the third is electrolysis of water and the fourth is the water-gas shift reaction.

questions.stem: After steam reforming, the gas mixture is reacted with more steam: CO(g) + H₂O(g) → CO₂(g) + H₂(g). What is the purpose of this water-gas shift step?
options: To convert carbon monoxide into extra hydrogen
To remove hydrogen so the reforming reaction speeds up
To convert carbon dioxide back into methane for reuse
To supply the heat needed by the reforming reaction
questions.explanation: The shift reaction uses the carbon monoxide from reforming to make more hydrogen, leaving carbon dioxide, which is separated out. Overall, CH₄ + 2H₂O → CO₂ + 4H₂.

questions.stem: Steam reforming, CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g), is endothermic. Why is it run at a high temperature, around 800 °C?
options: High temperature condenses the steam so that it reacts more readily
High temperature increases both the rate and the equilibrium yield of hydrogen
High temperature increases the rate but lowers the equilibrium yield of hydrogen
High temperature is needed to stop the nickel catalyst from working too fast
questions.explanation: For an endothermic reaction, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right, and it also speeds up the reaction. This differs from an exothermic process such as the Haber process, where high temperature lowers the yield.

questions.stem: Why does a low pressure favour the equilibrium yield of hydrogen in steam reforming, CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g)?
options: Low pressure lowers the activation energy of the forward reaction
There are 4 mol of gas on the product side and 2 mol on the reactant side
There are 2 mol of gas on the product side and 4 mol on the reactant side
Low pressure increases the rate of the forward reaction more than the reverse
questions.explanation: Lowering the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with more moles of gas, which is the product side (1 + 3 = 4 mol against 1 + 1 = 2 mol). Pressure changes do not alter the activation energy.

questions.stem: Overall, steam reforming followed by the water-gas shift gives CH₄ + 2H₂O → CO₂ + 4H₂. What mass of hydrogen can be made from 1.00 kg of methane? M: CH₄ 16.04, H₂ 2.016 g/mol.
questions.explanation: n(CH₄) = 1000/16.04 = 62.3 mol, so n(H₂) = 4 × 62.3 = 249 mol and m = 249 × 2.016 = 503 g. Using the 1:3 ratio of the reforming step alone gives 377 g.

questions.stem: In a trial, 32.08 g of methane is converted by CH₄ + 2H₂O → CO₂ + 4H₂, and 12.9 g of hydrogen is collected. What is the percentage yield? M: CH₄ 16.04, H₂ 2.016 g/mol.
questions.explanation: n(CH₄) = 2.000 mol, so the theoretical n(H₂) = 8.000 mol and m = 16.13 g. Yield = 12.9/16.13 × 100 = 80.0%. Comparing the mass of hydrogen with the mass of methane gives 40.2%, which is not a yield.

questions.stem: What is the atom economy for hydrogen in CH₄ + 2H₂O → CO₂ + 4H₂? M: CH₄ 16.04, H₂O 18.02, H₂ 2.016 g/mol.
questions.explanation: Atom economy = mass of desired product / total mass of reactants × 100 = (4 × 2.016)/(16.04 + 2 × 18.02) × 100 = 8.064/52.08 × 100 = 15.5%. Most of the mass of the reactants ends up as carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the production of hydrogen by electrolysis of water?
options: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)
H₂O(l) → H₂(g) + O(g)
H₂O(l) → H₂O₂(aq) + H₂(g)
2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
questions.explanation: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to decompose water into hydrogen and oxygen gases in a 2:1 mole ratio. The reverse reaction is what happens in a hydrogen fuel cell or when hydrogen burns.

questions.stem: During the electrolysis of water, at which electrode is hydrogen produced, and why?
options: At the anode, where water is reduced
At the cathode, where water is reduced
At the anode, where water is oxidised
At the cathode, where water is oxidised
questions.explanation: Hydrogen forms when hydrogen in water (oxidation number +1) gains electrons to become H₂ (oxidation number 0). Reduction occurs at the cathode in every electrochemical cell; oxygen forms at the anode by oxidation.

questions.stem: What mass of hydrogen is produced when 90.0 g of water is completely electrolysed? M: H₂O 18.02, H₂ 2.016 g/mol.
questions.explanation: n(H₂O) = 90.0/18.02 = 4.99 mol, and the 2:2 ratio gives 4.99 mol of H₂, which is 4.99 × 2.016 = 10.1 g. Halving the moles gives 5.03 g, and 79.9 g is the mass of oxygen produced.

questions.stem: Which method of producing hydrogen best meets green chemistry principles?
options: Gasification of coal with steam at high temperature
Electrolysis of water powered by a coal-fired power station
Electrolysis of water powered by solar or wind electricity
Steam reforming of natural gas with the CO₂ released to the air
questions.explanation: Water is a renewable raw material, and with renewable electricity the process releases no carbon dioxide and its by-product, oxygen, is harmless. The other methods depend on fossil fuels and release carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Biogas from the anaerobic digestion of food waste is mostly methane. Why is steam reforming of biogas considered a more sustainable source of hydrogen than reforming natural gas?
options: The methane comes from a renewable organic source rather than a fossil deposit
Biogas methane reacts with steam without releasing any carbon dioxide gas at all
Biogas contains hydrogen gas already, so no chemical reaction is needed
Biogas methane needs no catalyst because it is more reactive than natural gas
questions.explanation: The same reforming chemistry applies, but the methane comes from recently grown biomass, a renewable raw material, instead of a non-renewable fossil reserve. Carbon dioxide is still produced in the reaction.

questions.stem: A company captures and stores the CO₂ from its steam-reforming plant. Which green chemistry principle does the process still NOT meet?
options: Minimising unwanted products, because no carbon dioxide is formed
Limiting harmful solvents, because the process uses large volumes of them
Maximising yield, because the hydrogen is all lost in storage
Using renewable raw materials, because the methane is a fossil fuel
questions.explanation: Capturing the carbon dioxide stops it reaching the atmosphere, but the feedstock is still non-renewable natural gas. Carbon dioxide is still formed; it is simply stored instead of released.

questions.stem: What is molecular manufacturing?
options: Making products by grinding bulk materials down into tiny particles smaller than 100 nm
Making products by mixing reactants in large vats and separating the products
Making products by melting and moulding polymers into the shapes needed
Making products by positioning molecules precisely so that a specific reaction occurs
questions.explanation: Molecular manufacturing controls where molecules are, so that only the desired reaction happens at the desired place. Grinding bulk material down is a top-down approach, while molecular manufacturing builds products from the bottom up.

questions.stem: Why is protein synthesis in a cell an example of molecular manufacturing?
options: Enzymes melt amino acids together into a single long chain
A ribosome holds amino acids in position so a peptide bond forms in a set order
Amino acids collide at random in the cytoplasm until the right protein forms
Proteins are made by breaking down larger proteins eaten in the diet
questions.explanation: The ribosome brings each amino acid, carried by its transfer RNA, into exactly the right position next to the growing chain, so a condensation reaction joins them in the sequence coded by the messenger RNA.

questions.stem: Nanomaterials contain particles in which size range?
options: 1 to 100 µm
1 to 100 nm
questions.explanation: Nanomaterials have particles from 1 to 100 nanometres across, which gives them properties related to their size. A single atom is about 0.1 nm across, so 0.01 nm is smaller than an atom.

questions.stem: What is the structure of a carbon nanotube?
options: A long chain of carbon atoms joined by alternating single and triple bonds
A hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms arranged in hexagons and pentagons
A sheet of carbon atoms in hexagons, each bonded to three others, rolled into a cylinder
A tetrahedral network of carbon atoms, each bonded to four others, shaped into a hollow tube
questions.explanation: A nanotube is like a single layer of graphite (graphene) rolled into a seamless tube. A tetrahedral network describes diamond, and a hollow sphere of 60 atoms is buckminsterfullerene.

questions.stem: Carbon nanotubes have a very high tensile strength. What explains this?
options: Every carbon atom is joined to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds along the tube
Weak dispersion forces between the tubes stretch rather than break under load
Delocalised electrons move along the tube and hold the atoms in place
Metal catalyst atoms trapped inside the tube reinforce the structure
questions.explanation: The tube is one continuous covalent network, so pulling it apart means breaking many strong carbon-carbon bonds. Dispersion forces between separate tubes are weak by comparison.

questions.stem: Many carbon nanotubes conduct electricity along their length. What explains this?
options: Each carbon is bonded to three others, leaving electrons delocalised along the tube
Each carbon is bonded to four others, so its electrons are free to move
The tubes contain carbon ions that move through the hollow centre
The tubes absorb water from the air, which carries the current
questions.explanation: As in graphite, each carbon uses three electrons in covalent bonds, and the fourth is delocalised across the structure and free to move. In diamond, all four electrons are in bonds, so it does not conduct.

questions.stem: In one method, carbon nanotubes are grown by passing a carbon-containing gas over metal nanoparticles at high temperature. What role do the metal nanoparticles play?
options: They catalyse the breakdown of the gas and act as sites where the tubes grow
They react with the carbon to form a metal carbide that becomes the tube
They absorb oxygen from the gas so that the carbon does not burn
They melt and coat the outside of the tubes to make them conduct
questions.explanation: The nanoparticles catalyse the decomposition of the carbon-containing gas, and carbon atoms assemble into a tube at each particle. The size of the particle helps control the tube's diameter.

questions.stem: Which is a proposed medical use of nanorobots?
options: Removing the need for any further medical tests once they are injected
Copying themselves endlessly to replace the body's own cells
Carrying a drug through the body and releasing it only at diseased cells
Replacing a damaged organ with a complete artificial organ grown overnight
questions.explanation: Researchers are developing nanoscale devices that could carry a drug to a target, such as a tumour, and release it there, reducing side effects. Most such devices are still experimental.

questions.stem: A medical glucose sensor uses the enzyme glucose oxidase. Why is the enzyme used?
options: It stores glucose so the sensor can release it when blood glucose is low
It changes colour in proportion to the blood's pH, which shows the glucose
It catalyses a reaction of glucose only, producing a signal that can be measured
It converts every sugar in the blood into glucose so it can be measured
questions.explanation: Enzymes are highly selective, so glucose oxidase reacts with glucose but not with other substances in the blood. The reaction produces a substance that the sensor detects electrochemically, and the size of the signal shows the glucose concentration.

questions.stem: Why can coating a chemical sensor with nanoparticles make it more sensitive?
options: Their large surface area to volume ratio gives many more sites where the target can bind
Their small size makes each particle heavier, so binding is easier to detect
They slow down the reaction, giving the sensor more time to measure it
They react with every substance in the sample, so no target is missed
questions.explanation: Breaking a material into nanoparticles greatly increases its surface area for the same mass, so more target molecules can bind and produce a larger signal. A sensor must still be selective, not react with everything.

questions.stem: Why might molecular manufacturing support the green chemistry aim of minimising unwanted products?
options: Molecular manufacturing works only with harmful solvents, which dissolve waste
Positioning molecules makes every reaction go to completion in one second
Positioning molecules precisely allows only the desired reaction, reducing side products
Molecular manufacturing uses only fossil fuels as raw materials, which are cheaper to obtain
questions.explanation: When reactants are held in exactly the right position, the intended bond forms and competing reactions are avoided, so less waste is made. Using renewable raw materials and limiting harmful solvents are separate principles.

questions.stem: Before nanomaterials are widely used in medicine, why must their risks be evaluated carefully?
options: Their large size stops the body from removing them, so they always block blood vessels
They are made of elements that do not occur naturally anywhere in the human body
They lose all their special properties once they are inside the body
Their tiny size may let them enter cells and organs, and long-term effects are unclear
questions.explanation: Particles of 1 to 100 nm can cross barriers that larger particles cannot, and size-related properties may also bring unexpected effects. Because long-term data are limited, risks must be weighed against benefits.
